analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: A paid family leave bill with 208 House cosponsors was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would have created a federal insurance program, run through the Social Security Administration, paying workers two-thirds of their regular pay (capped at $4,000 a month) for up to 60 days when they need leave for a new child, their own serious illness, or to care for a family member. It would be funded by a 0.2% payroll tax on both employees and employers (0.4% for self-employed people). It would also make it illegal to fire or penalize a worker for applying for or using the benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need time off for the birth or adoption of a child, their own serious health condition, or care for a seriously ill family member, including domestic partners. Low earners would be protected by a minimum monthly benefit of $580, and the program covers workers regardless of whether their employer offers any paid leave today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers needing family or medical leave

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible worker would be entitled to a monthly benefit equal to two-thirds of regular pay, capped at $4,000 per month, for up to 60 days of qualified caregiving, with a minimum monthly benefit of $580.

Qualified caregiving covers the same reasons as the Family and Medical Leave Act: a worker's own serious health condition, birth or adoption of a child, and care for a spouse, child, or parent, with domestic partners explicitly included.

The program would be administered by a new Office of Paid Family and Medical Leave inside the Social Security Administration, and would coordinate with existing state paid leave programs without preempting stronger state laws.
It would be unlawful to fire, discipline, or discriminate against a worker for applying for or receiving benefits, with court remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees.
Funding comes from a 0.2% tax on wages paid equally by employees and employers (0.4% on self-employment income), deposited in a dedicated trust fund.

analysis.who_pays: All employers and employees, through a new 0.2% payroll tax on wages, and self-employed people, through a 0.4% tax, whether or not they ever take leave. Employers who already provide paid leave would pay the tax on top of their existing obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: All employers, employees, and self-employed workers

drawbacks.text: Every worker and employer pays the new payroll tax from the start, including people who never take a day of qualified leave, and the tax applies to all covered wages with no exemption for small employers.

Benefits are limited to 60 caregiving days per benefit period, shorter than the 12 weeks of job-protected (though unpaid) leave already guaranteed under the Family and Medical Leave Act, so workers with longer recoveries would run out of benefits.

The bill provides benefit payments and anti-retaliation protections but does not itself create the job-protected leave structure of the FMLA, and employers keep their existing obligations under collective bargaining agreements only if those provide greater benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: a national floor of paid leave that the United States, unlike most wealthy countries, does not have, covering childbirth, serious illness, and family caregiving with a genuine anti-retaliation enforcement regime. The cost is real but small by payroll-tax standards — about 0.4% of wages split between workers and employers — though it falls on everyone regardless of use, and the 60-day cap leaves longer recoveries uncovered. On balance the bill delivers considerably more to working people than it costs them, which is precisely why it needed broad committee support it never received.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, with 208 House cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and then to its Subcommittee on Worker and Family Support; that was the last action ever taken on it.
No committee vote, hearing record, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and self-employed workers avoided the new payroll tax, while workers without paid leave gained nothing; the bill's cosponsor list showed majority-party support, but the committee chair never moved it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the new payroll tax

sides.party_line_note: All 208 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 0.2% excise tax on every employer's payroll to fund the leave trust fund, with no exemption for firms that already offer paid leave. Because the tax funds benefits workers would receive, employers' interest in the bill ran against the workers the bill served.

Self-employed people would pay a higher 0.4% tax on their income but would gain access to paid leave benefits they currently can rarely obtain, since the program covers self-employment income and the bill covers leave for domestic partners too.

industries.industry: State paid family leave programs (California, New Jersey, New York, and others)
industries.note: The bill would not preempt state paid leave laws and would coordinate benefits with them, so states with existing programs keep their systems while their residents can supplement with the federal benefit.
